classification.difficultyReason: Rearrange the addition rule, use the upper bound on the union to find the least overlap, and recognise that the bound is attainable.

content.prompt: Let $P(A)=0.4$ and $P(B)=0.7$ be the probabilities of events $A$ and $B$ respectively.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Explain why $A$ and $B$ cannot be mutually exclusive events.

answer.short: If the events were mutually exclusive, their union would have probability $1.1$, which is impossible.
answer.worked:
Mutually exclusive events have $P(A\cap B)=0$. The addition rule would then give
$$\begin{align*}P(A\cup B)&=0.4+0.7\\ P(A\cup B)&=1.1.\end{align*}$$
A probability cannot exceed 1, so the events must overlap.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Find the smallest possible value of $P(A\cap B)$.

answer.short:
$0.1$.

The smallest overlap occurs when the union has probability 1.
answer.worked:
By the addition rule,
$$\begin{align*}P(A\cap B)&=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cup B)\\ P(A\cap B)&=1.1-P(A\cup B)\\ P(A\cap B)&\ge 1.1-1\\ P(A\cap B)&\ge 0.1.\end{align*}$$
This bound is possible. Probabilities of $0.3$ in $A$ only, $0.1$ in both and $0.6$ in $B$ only give the required event probabilities and a union of probability 1.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Find $P(A\cup B)$ when $P(A\cap B)$ is as small as possible.

answer.worked:
Use the minimum overlap of $0.1$ from part (b).
$$\begin{align*}P(A\cup B)&=0.4+0.7-0.1\\ P(A\cup B)&=1.\end{align*}$$
